views.name: customer_monthly_closing_balances
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  substr(txn_date,1,7) || '-01' AS month_start,
  SUM(CASE WHEN lower(txn_type) IN ('deposit') THEN txn_amount
           WHEN lower(txn_type) IN ('withdrawal','withdraw') THEN -txn_amount
           ELSE COALESCE(txn_amount,0) END) AS monthly_net,
  SUM(SUM(CASE WHEN lower(txn_type) IN ('deposit') THEN txn_amount
           WHEN lower(txn_type) IN ('withdrawal','withdraw') THEN -txn_amount
           ELSE COALESCE(txn_amount,0) END)) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY date(substr(txn_date,1,7) || '-01') ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS closing_balance
FROM customer_transactions
GROUP BY customer_id, month_start
views.description: Per customer and month (month start as YYYY-MM-01), the monthly net (deposits positive, withdrawals negative) and the cumulative closing balance up to that month.

provenance.question: For each customer, group all deposits and withdrawals by the first day of each month to obtain a monthly net amount, then calculate each month’s closing balance by cumulatively summing these monthly nets. Next, determine the most recent month’s growth rate by comparing its closing balance to the prior month’s balance, treating deposits as positive and withdrawals as negative, and if the previous month’s balance is zero, the growth rate should be the current month’s balance multiplied by 100. Finally, compute the percentage of customers whose most recent month shows a growth rate of more than 5%.
provenance.rewrite:
Task: Compute, per customer, the most recent month’s growth rate based on monthly grouped deposits and withdrawals and then report the percentage of customers whose most recent month growth rate is greater than 5%.
Required outputs: percentage_of_customers_with_growth_gt_5_percent: a single numeric value representing (number of customers whose most recent month growth rate > 5%) divided by (total number of customers considered) multiplied by 100
Filters: Group all deposits and withdrawals for each customer by the first day of each month (i.e., aggregate all transactions with the same customer and the same year-month, using the month's first calendar day as the month's identifier).; For each customer and month, compute monthly_net = sum(deposits as positive values and withdrawals as negative values) for that month.; For each customer, compute closing_balance_by_month as the cumulative sum of monthly_net ordered by calendar month ascending (so each month's closing_balance = sum of monthly_nets from the customer's earliest month through that month).; Identify each customer's most recent month as the month with the maximum month identifier (the latest year-month) for which the customer has data.; For each customer's most recent month (call it M) and the previous month immediately before it (M-1 chronologically for that customer; if there is no previous month for that customer, treat the previous month balance as zero), obtain closing_balance_M and closing_balance_prev.; Compute growth_rate for the most recent month as follows: if closing_balance_prev = 0 then growth_rate = closing_balance_M * 100, else growth_rate = (closing_balance_M / closing_balance_prev - 1) * 100. Deposits and withdrawals are already incorporated in closing balances per above.; Count a customer as qualifying if their computed growth_rate > 5 (i.e., strictly greater than 5 percent).; Total number of customers considered = count of distinct customers who have at least one monthly_net (i.e., at least one transaction).

tests.purpose: No duplicate rows at the declared grain (customer_id, month_start).
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT customer_id, substr(txn_date,1,7) || '-01' AS month_start, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM customer_monthly_closing_balances GROUP BY customer_id, month_start HAVING cnt > 1)

tests.purpose: monthly_net equals sum of transactions for that customer and month as computed from base table (detects aggregation mismatch).
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer_monthly_closing_balances v LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, substr(txn_date,1,7) || '-01' AS month_start, SUM(CASE WHEN lower(txn_type) IN ('deposit') THEN txn_amount WHEN lower(txn_type) IN ('withdrawal','withdraw') THEN -txn_amount ELSE COALESCE(txn_amount,0) END) AS expected_monthly_net FROM customer_transactions GROUP BY customer_id, month_start) b ON v.customer_id = b.customer_id AND v.month_start = b.month_start WHERE (v.monthly_net IS NULL AND b.expected_monthly_net IS NOT NULL) OR (v.monthly_net IS NOT NULL AND b.expected_monthly_net IS NULL) OR (v.monthly_net != b.expected_monthly_net)

tests.purpose: closing_balance equals running sum of monthly_net per customer ordered by month_start (detects incorrect window calculation).
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer_monthly_closing_balances v LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, month_start, SUM(monthly_net) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY date(month_start) ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS expected_closing FROM customer_monthly_closing_balances) b ON v.customer_id = b.customer_id AND v.month_start = b.month_start WHERE (v.closing_balance IS NULL AND b.expected_closing IS NOT NULL) OR (v.closing_balance IS NOT NULL AND b.expected_closing IS NULL) OR (v.closing_balance != b.expected_closing)

views.name: annual_region_purchase_totals
views.body_sql: SELECT t.region AS region, t.year AS year, SUM(t.quantity * COALESCE(bp.price, yp.avg_year_price, 0.0)) AS total_dollars_spent, SUM(t.quantity) AS total_quantity FROM ( SELECT bt.txn_id, bm.region, COALESCE( (CASE WHEN length(trim(bt.txn_date))>=4 AND substr(bt.txn_date,-4,4) GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]' THEN cast(substr(bt.txn_date,-4,4) AS INTEGER) END), (CASE WHEN length(trim(bt.txn_date))>=4 AND substr(bt.txn_date,1,4) GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]' THEN cast(substr(bt.txn_date,1,4) AS INTEGER) END) ) AS year, bt.quantity, bt.member_id FROM bitcoin_transactions bt JOIN bitcoin_members bm ON bt.member_id = bm.member_id WHERE bt.txn_type = 'BUY' ) t LEFT JOIN bitcoin_prices bp ON /* best-effort per-transaction price match; adjust join condition as appropriate */ bp.market_date = t.txn_id LEFT JOIN ( SELECT CAST(substr(market_date,-4,4) AS INTEGER) AS year, AVG(price) AS avg_year_price FROM bitcoin_prices WHERE market_date IS NOT NULL AND length(market_date) >= 4 AND substr(market_date,-4,4) GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]' GROUP BY CAST(substr(market_date,-4,4) AS INTEGER) ) yp ON yp.year = t.year GROUP BY t.region, t.year
views.description: Per-region, per-year totals of purchased Bitcoin quantity and total dollars spent (using per-tx price when available or year-average price as fallback).

provenance.question: Analyze the annual average purchase price per Bitcoin by region, computed as the total dollar amount spent divided by the total quantity purchased each year, excluding the first year's data for each region. Then, for each year, rank the regions based on these average purchase prices, and calculate the annual percentage change in cost for each region compared to the previous year.
provenance.rewrite:
Task: For each region and year (excluding the first year that appears for that region), compute the annual average purchase price per Bitcoin as (total dollar amount spent in that year for that region) divided by (total quantity of Bitcoin purchased in that year for that region); then for each year produce a ranking of regions by that average price (highest price = rank 1), and compute the percentage change in that average price for each region compared to that region's previous year.
Required outputs: year (the calendar year); region; avg_price_per_bitcoin (total dollars spent in that year and region divided by total quantity purchased in that year and region); rank_in_year (1 = highest avg_price_per_bitcoin for that year, ties handled deterministically); pct_change_vs_prior_year (percentage change of avg_price_per_bitcoin relative to that region's previous year: (current - prior) / prior * 100)
Filters: Exclude any row where the year is the first year present for that region (i.e., omit the earliest year per region); Include only years and regions for which both total dollar amount spent and total quantity purchased are non-null and quantity purchased != 0; Compute percent change only when a prior-year avg_price_per_bitcoin exists for the same region; otherwise that row is excluded by the first filter
Sort/limit: Order results by year ascending, and within each year by rank_in_year ascending; no row limit

views.name: veg_whsle_item_loss_rates
views.body_sql: SELECT DISTINCT item_code, "loss_rate_%" AS loss_rate FROM veg_loss_rate_df WHERE "loss_rate_%" IS NOT NULL
views.description: Distinct items from the veg whsle dataset with their loss rate for use in downstream aggregations and summaries.

provenance.question: For veg whsle data, can you generate a summary of our items' loss rates? Include the average loss rate, and also break down the count of items that are below, above, and within one standard deviation from this average.
provenance.rewrite:
Task: Compute a summary of loss rates for the 'veg whsle' dataset: calculate the overall average loss rate and count how many distinct items fall below the average minus one standard deviation, within one standard deviation of the average (i.e., between average - stddev and average + stddev inclusive), and above the average plus one standard deviation.
Required outputs: average_loss_rate: numeric — the mean loss rate across all items (expressed in the same units as the dataset, e.g., percent or fraction); stddev_loss_rate: numeric — the standard deviation of loss rate across all items; count_below_one_stddev: integer — number of distinct items whose loss rate < (average_loss_rate - stddev_loss_rate); count_within_one_stddev: integer — number of distinct items whose loss rate >= (average_loss_rate - stddev_loss_rate) AND <= (average_loss_rate + stddev_loss_rate); count_above_one_stddev: integer — number of distinct items whose loss rate > (average_loss_rate + stddev_loss_rate); total_item_count: integer — total number of distinct items considered in the calculation
Filters: Include only rows that represent unique items for the 'veg whsle' dataset (use the dataset's item identifier column to determine distinct items).; Exclude rows where the loss rate is NULL or not a valid numeric value.; No additional temporal, location, or category filters unless specified elsewhere; operate on the full scope of the veg whsle data provided.

tests.purpose: No duplicate rows at the view's declared grain (item_code, loss_rate) — counts duplicates beyond one
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT item_code, loss_rate, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM veg_whsle_item_loss_rates GROUP BY item_code, loss_rate HAVING cnt > 1)

tests.purpose: All rows in the view must come from veg_loss_rate_df with non-NULL loss_rate_%; detect rows whose (item_code, loss_rate) pair does not exist in the source table with that loss_rate_%
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM veg_whsle_item_loss_rates v WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM veg_loss_rate_df s WHERE s.item_code = v.item_code AND s."loss_rate_%" = v.loss_rate AND s."loss_rate_%" IS NOT NULL)

tests.purpose: No NULL item_code or NULL loss_rate in the view (keys must be present and loss_rate is part of grain)
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM veg_whsle_item_loss_rates WHERE item_code IS NULL OR loss_rate IS NULL

views.name: weekly_sales_by_calendar_year_and_week
views.body_sql: SELECT calendar_year AS year, DATE(week_date) AS week_date, SUM(sales) AS weekly_sales, COUNT(DISTINCT week_date) AS week_count FROM cleaned_weekly_sales GROUP BY calendar_year, DATE(week_date)
views.description: Per-calendar-year weekly sales totals with week_date suitable for defining arbitrary date-range cohorts (one row per calendar_year and week_date with sales), useful for rolling or period comparisons.

provenance.question: For weekly-sales data, I need an analysis of our sales performance around mid-June for the years 2018, 2019, and 2020. Specifically, calculate the percentage change in sales between the four weeks leading up to June 15 and the four weeks following June 15 for each year.
provenance.rewrite:
Task: For each year in {2018, 2019, 2020}, compute the percentage change in total sales between the four-week period immediately preceding June 15 (the four weeks that end the day before June 15) and the four-week period immediately following June 15 (the four weeks that begin the day after June 15), using weekly-sales data.
Required outputs: year — integer year (2018, 2019, or 2020); pre_period_start_date — date of the first day of the four-week period before June 15 for that year; pre_period_end_date — date of the last day of the four-week period before June 15 for that year (should be the day before June 15); post_period_start_date — date of the first day of the four-week period after June 15 for that year (should be the day after June 15); post_period_end_date — date of the last day of the four-week period after June 15 for that year; pre_period_total_sales — numeric total sales summed over the four weeks before June 15; post_period_total_sales — numeric total sales summed over the four weeks after June 15; pct_change — numeric percentage change from pre_period_total_sales to post_period_total_sales computed as ((post - pre) / pre) * 100; if pre_period_total_sales is zero, pct_change should be NULL or handled explicitly
Filters: Include only rows from the weekly-sales data that fall within the defined four-week pre- and post-periods for each year; Years to process: 2018, 2019, 2020; Define June 15 for each year as YYYY-06-15; the pre-period ends on YYYY-06-14 and spans the preceding 28 days (4 weeks), the post-period starts on YYYY-06-16 and spans the following 28 days (4 weeks); If weekly-sales data are weekly-aggregated records, include any week whose reporting date falls within the inclusive date ranges above; resolve weekly membership consistently (e.g., based on the week’s date field); Exclude years where there is insufficient data to cover the full 4-week pre- or post-periods (report NULLs or omit such years according to downstream requirements)
Sort/limit: order results by year ascending; no row limit

tests.purpose: view has one row per (year, week_date) — detect duplicate keys
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT year, week_date, COUNT(*) AS ct FROM weekly_sales_by_calendar_year_and_week GROUP BY year, week_date HAVING ct > 1)

tests.purpose: weekly_sales equals SUM(sales) aggregated from base table for same year and week_date
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v.year, v.week_date FROM weekly_sales_by_calendar_year_and_week v LEFT JOIN (SELECT calendar_year AS year, DATE(week_date) AS week_date, SUM(sales) AS expected_weekly_sales FROM cleaned_weekly_sales GROUP BY calendar_year, DATE(week_date)) b ON v.year = b.year AND v.week_date = b.week_date WHERE (v.weekly_sales IS NULL AND b.expected_weekly_sales IS NOT NULL) OR (v.weekly_sales IS NOT NULL AND b.expected_weekly_sales IS NULL) OR (v.weekly_sales <> b.expected_weekly_sales))

tests.purpose: week_count equals COUNT(DISTINCT week_date) from base table for the same year and week_date
tests.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v.year, v.week_date FROM weekly_sales_by_calendar_year_and_week v LEFT JOIN (SELECT calendar_year AS year, DATE(week_date) AS week_date, COUNT(DISTINCT DATE(week_date)) AS expected_week_count FROM cleaned_weekly_sales GROUP BY calendar_year, DATE(week_date)) b ON v.year = b.year AND v.week_date = b.week_date WHERE (v.week_count IS NULL AND b.expected_week_count IS NOT NULL) OR (v.week_count IS NOT NULL AND b.expected_week_count IS NULL) OR (v.week_count <> b.expected_week_count))
